kiln_guide.text: Welcome to Gladstone! A whole Victorian potbank, kept just as it was, with its bottle ovens round the yard.
The bottle shape is the hovel, a brick chimney round the real oven inside. It drew the smoke up and out, over everybody's washing.
Placers, firemen, saggar makers, mould makers, throwers, turners, dippers, paintresses. A single teacup went through a dozen pairs of hands.

loo_guide.text: Welcome to Flushed with Pride! Our gallery of the history of the toilet. Yes, really. Stoke made the nation's loos.
Thomas Twyford of Hanley sold one of the first one-piece china toilets, the Unitas, in 1883. Before that, most were wood boxes round a metal pan. Grim.
And no, Thomas Crapper did not invent the toilet. He just sold a lot of them with his name on. Very good branding.

thrower.text: Watch the clay. Centre it first, or it'll wobble off and hit you in the face. Ask me how I know.
Most Stoke ware was made in moulds, not thrown. But the wheel's the bit visitors love, so I get to show off.
